title: Aligning HR with Business Strategy
objective: Talk about how HR supports business goals, using natural business English at intermediate level.
grammarDetail: Present Perfect vs Past Simple. Use the Present Perfect for experiences or changes connected to now: HR has become more strategic. Use the Past Simple for finished moments: We launched the new plan last March.
grammarDeepDive: The Present Perfect and the Past Simple are two of the most important tenses in business English, and one of the hardest pairs for Portuguese speakers. At Czarnikow, you use both every day — in emails, reports and meetings — so mastering the difference is essential for sounding natural and professional. The Past Simple describes a finished action at a specific time in the past: We launched the programme last March. She joined the company in 2019. The key word is finished — the action is over, and we know when it happened. The Present Perfect connects a past action or experience to the present moment: We have reduced turnover by 30%. title: Designing an Organisational Structure
objective: Describe reporting lines, team structures and organisational change at intermediate level.
grammarDetail: Passive Voice — present. Very common in business: Decisions are made at team level. A new model is being implemented this quarter. Structure: be + past participle .
grammarDeepDive: The passive voice is one of the most important structures in business English. In reports, policies, organisational charts and process descriptions, the passive appears everywhere — because we often care more about what happens than who does it . At Czarnikow, you might read 'Decisions are made at regional level' or 'The structure is reviewed every two years'. Both are passive. The structure is simple: subject + be (am/is/are) + past participle . The 'doer' can be added with by , but is often omitted when it is obvious or unimportant. For actions happening right now, we use the present continuous passive: is/are being + past participle — as in 'A new reporting line is being created'. Eastwoo

title: Reading HR Metrics and KPIs
objective: Discuss HR data, trends and KPIs with confidence at intermediate level.
grammarDetail: Comparatives and superlatives. Use -er / more to compare and -est / most for the top. Example: Turnover is lower than last year. This is the highest engagement score we have ever recorded.
grammarDeepDive: In business, almost everything is about comparison: this quarter versus last quarter, our costs versus the industry average, one team's performance versus another's. That is why comparatives and superlatives are essential tools in every HR professional's language toolkit. At Czarnikow, when Harry presents the dashboard, nearly every sentence uses a comparative or a superlative to tell the story behind the numbers. The rules are straightforward. For short adjectives (one syllable), add -er for the comparative and -est for the superlative: low → lower → the lowest . title: Running a Fair Performance Review
objective: Lead a professional performance review and use reported speech to summarise what was said.
grammarDetail: Reported speech. When we report what someone said, we usually shift the tense back one step. Example: She said she was happy with her results. He told me he would apply for the senior role next year.
grammarDeepDive: In business, we constantly report what others have said — in emails, meeting notes, review summaries and feedback forms. At Czarnikow, after a performance review, Sophie writes notes like 'He said he was happy with his results' or 'She told me she would apply for the senior role next year' . This is reported speech, and it is essential for professional communication. The main rule is the tense shift : when we report past conversations, we usually move the tense back one step. 'I am proud' becomes 'She said she was proud' . 'I will apply' becomes 'He said he would apply' . 'I can do it' becomes 'She said she could do it' . title: Running a Professional Recruitment Process
objective: Describe a recruitment process step by step and give advice on best practices.
grammarDetail: Modals of advice and obligation. Use should for strong advice, must / have to for obligation, and could / might for softer suggestions. Example: You should always send feedback to rejected candidates. Every hire must be approved by the business owner.
grammarDeepDive: In recruitment — and in business generally — we constantly give advice, make recommendations and state obligations. The language of modals is what makes the difference between 'You check references' (flat statement) and 'You should always check references before the offer' (clear professional advice). At Czarnikow, Oliver uses modals every day when training new recruiters and advising hiring managers.  Should is for strong advice or best practice: 'You should send feedback within 48 hours.'  Could and might are for softer suggestions: 'You could consider an internal candidate first.'  Must and have to express obligation: 'Every offer must be approved by the business owner.' title: Behavioural and Competency-Based Interviews
objective: Ask and answer behavioural interview questions using the STAR method.
grammarDetail: Past Simple vs Past Continuous. STAR answers mix both: Past Simple for finished actions ( I called the client ) and Past Continuous for background actions ( while the team was finalising the proposal ).
grammarDeepDive: In behavioural interviews, you need to tell stories about the past. That means you need two tenses working together: the Past Simple for completed, finished actions ( I called the client , She accepted the offer ) and the Past Continuous for longer background actions that were in progress when something else happened ( While the team was finalising the proposal, the deadline moved forward ). Together, they create a vivid narrative — one thing was happening (continuous) and then another thing interrupted or happened at the same time (simple). title: Building a Strong Employer Brand
objective: Talk about employer branding campaigns, reputation and how companies attract talent.
grammarDetail: Present Perfect Continuous. Use for actions that started in the past and continue now, especially about trends: We have been investing in employer branding since 2022.
grammarDeepDive: When we talk about employer branding, we often describe actions that started in the past and are still happening now. That is exactly what the Present Perfect Continuous does. At Czarnikow, you might say 'We have been investing in employer branding since 2022' — the investment started in 2022 and it continues today. The emphasis is on the duration and the ongoing nature of the action, not on whether it is finished. The form is straightforward: have/has + been + verb-ing . Use have been with I/you/we/they and has been with he/she/it. title: A Professional Onboarding Journey
objective: Design and talk about a structured onboarding journey from day one to month six.
grammarDetail: First Conditional. Used for realistic future results: If we run a strong onboarding, new hires will be productive faster. If we skip the pre-boarding, the first day will feel cold.
grammarDeepDive: In HR, we constantly make proposals and predictions about realistic future outcomes. The First Conditional is the grammar we use for these situations: If we run a structured onboarding, new hires will be productive faster. The 'if' clause states a realistic condition (something that can really happen), and the 'will' clause states the expected result. This is not a dream — it is a plan. The structure is: If + subject + Present Simple, subject + will + base form . Notice that the if-clause uses the Present Simple , not 'will'. title: Designing Learning and Development Programmes
objective: Talk about L&D programmes, blended learning and changes in corporate training.
grammarDetail: Used to / would. Use used to for past habits and states: Training used to be all in person. Use would only for repeated past actions: We would spend whole days in classrooms.
grammarDeepDive: When we talk about how corporate training has changed, we need to describe how things used to be and what people would do in the past. Used to describes past habits and past states that are no longer true : Training used to be all in person — it was, but it is not any more. Would describes repeated past actions (but NOT states): We would spend whole days in classrooms — we did this regularly in the past, but we do not do it now. The key rule, as both Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) and Murphy ( English Grammar in Use ) explain, is that would  cannot be used for past states. You cannot say 'I would be a manager' to mean 'I was a manager in the past' — you must say 'I used to be a manager

title: Developing Leaders Across the Company
objective: Discuss leadership development, pipelines and the qualities of modern leaders.
grammarDetail: Second Conditional. Use for imagined or unlikely situations: If we invested more in coaching, we would see better leaders in two years.
grammarDeepDive: When we discuss leadership development, we often imagine situations that are not real yet — or that are unlikely. The Second Conditional is the grammar for these hypothetical scenarios: If we invested more in coaching, we would see better leaders in two years. The 'if' clause states an imagined condition (we are not investing more right now), and the 'would' clause states the imagined result. This is not a plan — it is a thought experiment. The structure is: If + subject + Past Simple, subject + would + base form . Notice that the if-clause uses the Past Simple , not 'would'. This is the mirror of the First Conditional rule. title: Career Pathing and Succession Planning
grammar: Future forms — will, going to, present continuous
objective: Discuss career paths, internal mobility and succession planning in clear intermediate English.
grammarDetail: Future forms. Use will for predictions and decisions made now, going to for plans already decided, and present continuous for scheduled events: She is joining the finance team in May. We are going to promote two managers next quarter. She'll probably be ready in twelve months.
grammarDeepDive: English has three main ways to talk about the future, and each one carries a different message. At Czarnikow, choosing the right form helps you sound precise and professional — especially in talent reviews and planning meetings where clarity about timing and certainty matters enormously.  Will is used for predictions, beliefs and decisions made at the moment of speaking: 'I think she'll be ready in twelve months' , 'I'll send you the succession list after the meeting.'  Going to is used for plans and intentions that are already decided: 'We're going to redesign the career paths this quarter — the budget is approved.' title: Coaching and Feedback Conversations
objective: Run a coaching conversation and give structured feedback using common business expressions.
grammarDetail: Gerunds and infinitives. Some verbs are followed by -ing ( avoid, enjoy, suggest ), others by to + infinitive ( decide, need, want ). Example: She avoids delegating. She needs to trust her team more.
grammarDeepDive: In English, when one verb follows another, the second verb takes either the -ing form (gerund) or the to + base form (infinitive). The choice depends on the first verb, and there is no simple rule — you must learn the patterns. This matters enormously in coaching and feedback conversations at Czarnikow, where precision in language signals professionalism and emotional intelligence. Some verbs always take the gerund: avoid, enjoy, suggest, keep, recommend, consider, mind . Others always take the infinitive: decide, need, want, agree, expect, plan, refuse, offer . title: Measuring and Boosting Engagement
objective: Talk about engagement surveys, pulse checks and how to act on the results.
grammarDetail: Phrasal verbs. Very common in business English: pick up on, act on, follow through, drop off, reach out, speak up. Learn them in context, not in isolation.
grammarDeepDive: Phrasal verbs are one of the most distinctive features of English, and they dominate everyday business conversations. A phrasal verb is a verb combined with one or two particles (prepositions or adverbs) that together create a meaning different from the individual words. At Czarnikow, you will hear them constantly in HR discussions: 'We need to act on this', 'Engagement has dropped off', 'Please follow through on your promises.'  There are two main types. Inseparable phrasal verbs keep the verb and particle together: act on, pick up on, follow through . You cannot put anything between them. title: Building and Protecting Company Culture
objective: Describe a company culture clearly and explain how behaviours and rituals shape it.
grammarDetail: Defining relative clauses. Used to define who or what we are talking about, with who, that, which : The behaviours that we reward become the real culture. The people who are promoted send the strongest signal.
grammarDeepDive: A defining relative clause gives essential information about who or what we are talking about. Without it, the sentence does not make sense or means something completely different. In business English at Czarnikow, relative clauses are everywhere: 'The people who are promoted send the strongest cultural signal' — remove 'who are promoted' and you lose the meaning entirely. Use who for people, which for things, and that for both. In defining clauses, that is very common in spoken English and often preferred in business writing because it sounds direct: 'The behaviours that we reward become the culture.' title: Diversity, Equity and Inclusion in Practice
objective: Discuss DEI initiatives, challenges and language to describe inclusive workplaces.
grammarDetail: Non-defining relative clauses. Add extra information with commas: Our DEI strategy, which was launched in 2023, focuses on inclusion. Our CEO, who chairs the DEI council, is personally involved.
grammarDeepDive: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about a noun that is already clearly identified. It is separated by commas and can be removed without changing the core meaning of the sentence. At Czarnikow, you use these constantly in reports and presentations: 'Our CEO, who chairs the DEI council, is personally involved.' We already know who the CEO is — the clause just adds a useful detail. The key rules are: use who for people and which for things — never that in non-defining clauses. Always use commas (or a comma and a full stop if the clause is at the end). Eastwood is very clear on this point: 'that' is only for defining clauses. title: Internal Communication That Actually Works
grammar: Linking words — however, therefore, in addition
objective: Explain internal communication strategies and write clear messages at intermediate level.
grammarDetail: Linking words. Use them to connect ideas: However (contrast), therefore (result), in addition (adding). Example: The policy is simple; however, its impact will be wide. Therefore, we need clear talking points. In addition, managers will receive training.
grammarDeepDive: Linking words are the glue of professional writing and speaking. They connect ideas, signal relationships between sentences and guide the reader or listener through your argument. In internal communications at Czarnikow, using the right linking word can mean the difference between a message that flows naturally and one that feels like a list of disconnected facts. The three most important linking words for business are however , therefore and in addition .  However signals contrast or unexpected information: The policy is straightforward; however, its rollout requires careful planning. title: Navigating Global Labour Laws
grammar: Modals of obligation — must, have to, be required to
objective: Discuss labour law differences across countries and explain compliance obligations.
grammarDetail: Obligation modals.  Must (strong, often written rules), have to (external obligation), be required to (formal, often legal). Example: In Germany, we are required to consult the works council. In Brazil, you have to pay the thirteenth salary.
grammarDeepDive: In business and especially in HR, talking about obligations is a daily necessity. Whether you are explaining what the law demands, what company policy requires, or what a manager needs to do, you need the right modal verb to express the right level of obligation. At Czarnikow, where teams operate across multiple jurisdictions, precision in obligation language is not just grammar — it is a legal and professional skill.  Must expresses strong obligation, often from rules, laws or the speaker's authority: Every contract must be in the local language. title: Compensation and Benefits Strategy
objective: Discuss salaries, benefits, pay bands and total rewards with business nuance.
grammarDetail: Comparatives with intensifiers. Use much, far, slightly, a little to make comparatives more precise. Example: Our bonus scheme is much more competitive. Base pay is slightly below market in one country.
grammarDeepDive: In business, especially in HR and compensation discussions, we constantly compare: salaries against the market, benefits packages against competitors, this year's bonus against last year's. Simple comparatives ( higher, lower, more competitive ) are a good start, but they lack precision. Adding an intensifier tells the listener how much bigger or smaller the difference is — and that precision matters when you are presenting to the board or negotiating with a candidate at Czarnikow.  Much and far signal a large difference: Our bonus is much higher than the market average. The total package is far more competitive than last year. title: Handling Conflicts and Difficult Conversations
grammar: Would / could for politeness and softeners
objective: Run a difficult conversation professionally, using diplomatic business English.
grammarDetail: Softeners. Use would, could, might, I wonder if to make sentences more diplomatic. Example: I would like to share how I saw the situation. Could we agree on what to try next?
grammarDeepDive: In business English, especially in HR, how you say something matters as much as what you say. A direct statement like 'You are wrong' may be factually accurate, but it shuts down conversation. Replace it with 'I wonder if we might see this differently' and you create space for dialogue. This is not weakness — it is strategy. At Czarnikow, where teams span cultures and countries, mastering diplomatic language is a core professional skill. The most common softeners are would ( I would like to discuss this ), could ( Could we find a different approach? ), might ( You might want to consider this ) and the phrase I wonder if ( I wonder if we could talk about what happened ). title: Remote and Hybrid Work Policies
objective: Discuss remote and hybrid policies, their challenges and their impact on teams.
grammarDetail: Third Conditional. Used for imagined past situations: If the pandemic hadn't happened, we wouldn't have adopted hybrid work so quickly. If we had kept the old policy, we would have lost talent.
grammarDeepDive: The Third Conditional is how English speakers talk about the past that didn't happen. It lets us reflect on decisions, imagine alternative outcomes and learn from experience. In an HR context at Czarnikow, it is invaluable: If we had introduced hybrid work sooner, we would have retained more talent during the pandemic. This sentence does two things — it acknowledges what actually happened and imagines a better alternative. That combination of hindsight and hypothesis is what makes the Third Conditional so powerful in professional discussions.
